title: Women's History Month: The Women Who Shaped Cannabis
h1: Women in Cannabis History: Herbalists, Activists, Scientists and Founders
metaDescription: Women in cannabis history, from medieval herbals and medical-era activists to scientists and founders, plus how to support women-owned brands in Michigan.
excerpt: For Women's History Month or any month: the women who shaped cannabis, what's legend and what's record, today's numbers and how to find women-owned brands in Michigan.
keyTakeaways: Women's History Month has been observed every March since Congress designated March 1987 as the first one.
The story that Queen Victoria used cannabis is popular, but historians have found no direct evidence for it.
Medical-era activists like Brownie Mary in San Francisco and Mae Nutt in Michigan pushed for seriously ill patients' access long before legal sales.

body:
Women in cannabis history are easy to overlook and hard to ignore once you start looking. Women kept herbal knowledge, organized care for seriously ill patients when cannabis was illegal, built key pieces of the science and now help run the legal industry. This guide separates the documented record from popular legends, looks at how women use cannabis today and shares practical ways to find women-owned cannabis brands in Michigan.

## Why women in cannabis history deserve the spotlight

Women's History Month is observed every March. According to the Library of Congress, it began as Women's History Week in 1982, and Congress designated March 1987 as the first Women's History Month. Presidents have issued a proclamation for it every year since 1995, and the next observance arrives in March 2027.

Every March, including Women's History Month 2025 and 2026, brings fresh attention to women in cannabis. The story runs much longer than one month, though. Women were often the caregivers, the patients' advocates and the keepers of plant knowledge, roles that rarely made it into official records.

That's why this history takes some digging, and why it's worth getting right. For today's founders and executives, see our companion piece on [women in the cannabis industry](/blog/women-in-cannabis/).

## Early medicine and folklore: what the record supports and what is legend

Cannabis history is full of good stories, and not all of them hold up. Here's how three popular ones compare with the record:

| Popular claim | What the record shows |
|---|---|
| A medieval abbess wrote about hemp | Hard to check online. Hildegard von Bingen's *Physica* describes the uses of more than 200 plants, but hemp quotes credited to her vary, so look for a scholarly translation |
| Queen Victoria used cannabis | No direct evidence. A physician to her household praised cannabis in a medical journal, but historians call the royal story a myth |
| Brownie Mary baked for AIDS patients | Well documented, including arrests and years of hospital volunteering |

Hildegard von Bingen (1098 to 1179) was a German abbess and writer. A University of Iowa library record of the first printed edition of *Physica* notes that she listed the merits of more than 200 plants, 50 kinds of trees and 20 precious stones. Her work is a reminder that women in religious houses and households kept and passed on practical plant knowledge. Be wary of dramatic quotes credited to her on social media, though, since translations vary.

The Queen Victoria story is the classic legend. Sir J. Russell Reynolds, a physician to the royal household, wrote favorably about cannabis preparations in The Lancet in the late 1800s. That much is real. But a history post from the Alcohol and Drugs History Society couldn't trace the claim to the Queen's diaries or correspondence, and historian James H. Mills, in his book *Cannabis Britannica*, found "no direct evidence" and called the claim a myth.

The lesson for any history month: enjoy the stories, but ask where they come from.

## Women activists of the medical cannabis era

Long before legal dispensaries, women were organizing to get cannabis to seriously ill people, often at real personal risk.

### Mae Nutt, Beaverton, Michigan

Mae Nutt lost two sons to cancer: Dana in 1967 and Keith in 1979. In the late 1970s she became an outspoken advocate for seriously ill patients' legal access to marijuana, and her campaign reached the Michigan Legislature in 1979. After Keith died, she ran an informal "Green Cross" from the family's Beaverton home, sharing his remaining supply with other patients. The family's papers, which document the advocacy of Mae, Keith and Arnold Nutt, are held by the University of Michigan Library.

### Mary Jane Rathbun, "Brownie Mary," San Francisco

Mary Jane Rathbun became famous for baking cannabis brownies for people with AIDS. For 16 years she visited the AIDS ward at San Francisco General Hospital every week, talking with patients and carrying specimens to the lab. She was arrested three times. After a 1992 arrest, prosecutors dropped the charges, and her activism helped build public support for Proposition 215, the 1996 California measure that legalized medical marijuana there. She died in 1999 at 77.

### Valerie Corral, Santa Cruz, California

Valerie Corral and her husband, Michael, led the Wo/Men's Alliance for Medical Marijuana, a patient collective near Santa Cruz. In September 2002, federal agents raided the group's farm. The Corrals were released without charges, and Santa Cruz's mayor led the city council in a symbolic handout to the patients the collective had served. The episode made the gap between state and federal law impossible to ignore.

## Researchers pushing for clinical evidence

Activism raised the questions. Researchers set out to answer them, and women did a lot of that work.

- **Allyn Howlett.** In 1988, a St. Louis University team that included pharmacologist Allyn Howlett and her student William Devane published the seminal paper characterizing a cannabinoid receptor in the brain. That finding opened the door to decades of research on how cannabinoids act in the body. Howlett later continued her work at Wake Forest.
- **Ziva Cooper.** Cooper directs the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids and studies how cannabis affects men and women differently. In a 2014 analysis with Margaret Haney at Columbia University, women matched with men for cannabis use gave higher ratings to some effects linked with misuse, such as wanting to take the drug again. Ratings of feeling high didn't differ.
- **Sue Sisley.** Sisley, a physician and psychiatrist in Scottsdale, Arizona, pushed for better research cannabis. She criticized the federal supply she received as a "powdery mishmash of stems, sticks and leaves" and sued the Drug Enforcement Administration over its slow handling of applications to grow cannabis for research. A 2020 suit settled when the government released the legal memo behind the delay.
- **Staci Gruber.** Gruber, a member of Harvard Medical School's psychiatry faculty, founded the Marijuana Investigations for Neuroscientific Discovery program at McLean Hospital. It studies medical cannabis use through long-term observational studies, surveys and clinical trials.

Work like this matters because men and women don't always respond to cannabis the same way. Knowing how responses differ helps everyone make better-informed choices.

## From activism to the legal market: a short bridge

Activists helped turn compassion into law. California's Proposition 215 passed in 1996, Michigan voters approved a medical marijuana program in 2008 and adult-use legalization followed in Michigan in 2018. Today women work across the legal business, from cultivation and lab work to compliance, marketing and the sales floor.

Some became firsts. Wanda James, a military veteran, and her husband became the first African Americans to own a cannabis company in America in 2009, according to her University of Colorado regent biography. She later became the first Black woman elected to that board in more than 44 years. Read more about her in our guide to [Black cannabis pioneers](/blog/black-cannabis-pioneers/).

How many businesses do women own today? The answer depends on the state. A 2026 George Washington University study of 17 adult-use states with equity programs found that, where states reported it, women held from 22% of cannabis licenses in Illinois to 44% in New Jersey. Industry surveys of women in executive roles have swung widely from year to year, so no single number tells the whole story.

## How women use cannabis today

Fewer women than men say they smoke cannabis, but plenty do. Gallup's combined 2023 and 2024 polling found that 15% of U.S. adults say they smoke marijuana, including 17% of men and 11% of women. That survey asked only about smoking, so it doesn't capture everyone who prefers edibles, vapes or other forms.

Research on sex differences is still young, which is one more reason to begin with a small amount of any new product and wait before having more. Every Michigan cannabis label carries a pregnancy and breastfeeding warning. If you're pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medications or managing a health condition, talk with a clinician before using cannabis.

Many women shop for themselves, for friends or for gifts. Our guides to [cannabis products for women](/blog/cannabis-products-for-women/) and [Mother's Day cannabis gifts](/blog/mothers-day-cannabis-gifts/) cover the options for adults 21 and older. And for another month that celebrates the people who shaped cannabis culture, see our look at [cannabis and Pride Month](/blog/cannabis-pride-month/).

## Finding and supporting women-owned brands in Michigan

Women-owned cannabis brands aren't always labeled as such, so a little homework helps:

1. **Start with the label.** Every Michigan cannabis package names the producer and its state license number, so you know which company to look up.
2. **Read the brand's own story.** A company website or about page usually names its founders. Look for who owns it today, too, since "women-founded" and "women-owned" aren't always the same thing.
3. **Ask at the counter.** Our budtenders at [High Society's Michigan stores](/dispensary-locations/) are happy to help you look into a brand and compare options.
4. **Look beyond March.** Buying from a brand you believe in matters most when it's steady, not seasonal.
5. **Support the bigger picture.** Mentorship, hiring and equity programs all shape who gets to build a business in this industry.

Selection varies by store and changes often, so check your store's menu for what's available today. Adults 21 and older, and registered medical patients 18 and older, can shop with a valid ID. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Who are famous women in cannabis history?
faq.a: Start with the activists: Brownie Mary baked for AIDS patients in San Francisco, Mae Nutt was an early medical advocate in Beaverton, Michigan, and Valerie Corral led a Santa Cruz patient collective. In science, Allyn Howlett's team characterized the brain's cannabinoid receptor in 1988. In business, Wanda James stands out. Many more worked without recognition.

Probably not, and there's no direct evidence she did. Sir J. Russell Reynolds, a physician to the royal household, wrote favorably about cannabis in The Lancet in the late 1800s, which likely fed the legend. Historians who went looking couldn't trace the claim to her diaries or letters, and historian James H. Mills calls the story a myth.

faq.q: What share of cannabis executives are women?
faq.a: It depends on the survey and the year. Industry polls of executive roles have shifted widely from year to year. License data gives a firmer picture: a 2026 George Washington University study found that, in states that reported it, women held from 22% of cannabis licenses in Illinois to 44% in New Jersey.

Mary Jane Rathbun, known as Brownie Mary, was a San Francisco volunteer who baked cannabis brownies for people with AIDS. For 16 years she visited the AIDS ward at San Francisco General Hospital each week. She was arrested three times, and her activism helped build support for California's 1996 medical marijuana measure. She died in 1999.

faq.q: How can I find women-owned cannabis brands in Michigan?
faq.a: Start with the producer named on the package, then read the company's own about page to learn who founded and owns it. Women-founded and women-owned can differ, so check both. You can also ask your budtender for help looking into a brand. Selection changes, so check your store's menu for what's available today.

claims.claim: Women's History Month began as Women's History Week in 1982; Congress designated March 1987 as the first Women's History Month; presidents have issued annual proclamations since 1995; observed every March since.
claims.evidence: "the week beginning March 7, 1982 as 'Women's History Week'"; "designated the month of March 1987 as 'Women's History Month'"; "Between 1988 and 1994, Congress passed additional resolutions"; "Since 1995, presidents have issued a series of annual proclamations".

claims.claim: The next observance arrives in March 2027.
claims.evidence: Observed every March; true as of the October 2026 publication.

claims.claim: Hildegard von Bingen (1098-1179), a German abbess, listed the merits of more than 200 plants, 50 kinds of trees and 20 precious stones in Physica (Iowa record of the 1533 first printed edition).
claims.evidence: "SAINT HILDEGARD (1098-1179). Physica. Strasbourg ... 1533"; "Abbess of a convent near Bingen in Germany"; "She lists the therapeutic merits of over 200 plants, 50 kinds of trees, and 20 precious stones."

claims.claim: Table: "cannabis histories often point to [Physica's] hemp entry".
claims.fix: The Iowa record does not mention hemp, and searches found no scholarly edition, translation or article that could be opened to confirm the hemp passage (only a non-scholarly blog). Cell reworded: "Hard to check online ... hemp quotes credited to her vary, so look for a scholarly translation", matching the body's caution about quotes.
claims.evidence: Iowa record lists plants, trees, stones, fish, birds, animals, reptiles and metals; no hemp mention.

claims.claim: No direct evidence that Queen Victoria used cannabis; a Points (Alcohol and Drugs History Society) post could not trace it to her diaries or correspondence; James H. Mills (Cannabis Britannica) found "no direct evidence" and called it a myth.
claims.evidence: "a mention of marijuana in the Queen's diaries or correspondence ... All I found, however, was a number of un-cited assertions"; "James H. Mills writes that there is 'no direct evidence' for the claim, going so far as to deem the claim ... a 'myth' (142)".

claims.claim: Sir J. Russell Reynolds, a physician to the royal household, wrote favorably about cannabis preparations in The Lancet in the late 1800s.
claims.evidence: Crossref record: J. Russell Reynolds, "On the therapeutical uses and toxic effects of Cannabis indica", The Lancet, March 1890. Points: "Queen Victoria's personal physician, J. Russell Reynolds, widely prescribed cannabis".

claims.claim: Mae Nutt lost two sons to cancer: Dana in 1967 and Keith in 1979.
claims.evidence: "two of her sons, Keith (December 21, 1955-October 20, 1979) and Dana (1958-1967) died from cancer".

claims.claim: In the late 1970s she became an advocate for patients' legal access, and her campaign reached the Michigan Legislature in 1979.
claims.evidence: "She began her crusade to legalize the medical use of marijuana before Keith died. On October 10, 1979, the Michigan House voted unanimously ... Five days later, the Senate agreed. Act No. 125 of the Public Acts of 1979".

claims.claim: After Keith died she ran an informal "Green Cross" from the family's Beaverton home, sharing his remaining supply with other patients.
claims.evidence: "Following Keith's death, Mae began operating a 'Green Cross' from the Nutts' home in Beaverton, Michigan, illegally distributing Keith's remaining marijuana to those needing it for medical relief."

claims.claim: The family's papers documenting Mae, Keith and Arnold Nutt's advocacy are held by the University of Michigan Library.
claims.evidence: "The rest of the collection documents Mae, and to a lesser extent, Keith and Arnold Nutt, and their efforts to legalize marijuana for medical or therapeutic use".

claims.claim: Brownie Mary visited the AIDS ward at San Francisco General Hospital every week for 16 years, talking with patients and carrying specimens to the lab.
claims.evidence: "each Thursday for 16 years ... would visit the AIDS ward at San Francisco General Hospital 'where she volunteered, visiting patients and carrying specimens to the lab.'"

claims.claim: She was arrested three times; after a 1992 arrest prosecutors dropped the charges.
claims.evidence: "gained national attention" after a 1992 arrest ... "The charges were dropped"; "Rathburn was arrested three times".

claims.claim: Her activism helped build public support for Proposition 215, the 1996 California measure that legalized medical marijuana there.
claims.evidence: "Her actions created a 'groundswell of support' for the eventual passage of Proposition 215, which legalized medical marijuana in California." Year: "California's 1996 medical-marijuana law, Proposition 215" (American Prospect).

claims.claim: She died in 1999 at 77.
claims.evidence: April 13, 1999 item: "died yesterday in San Francisco at age 77".

claims.claim: Valerie and Michael Corral led the Wo/Men's Alliance for Medical Marijuana, a patient collective near Santa Cruz.
claims.evidence: ACLU: "a Santa Cruz-area medical marijuana cooperative, the Wo/Men's Alliance for Medical Marijuana (WAMM)". (The cited American Prospect piece writes 'Association'; the group's name is Alliance.)

claims.claim: In September 2002 federal agents raided the group's farm; the Corrals were released without charges.
claims.evidence: "Early in the morning of Sept. 5, Drug Enforcement Administration officials raided a small farm near Santa Cruz"; the Corrals "were arrested following the raid and later released without being charged".

claims.claim: Santa Cruz's mayor led "a symbolic city hall handout" to the collective's patients.
claims.fix: The opened source describes the mayor leading the city council in a symbolic handout but does not place it at city hall. Reworded: "led the city council in a symbolic handout".
claims.evidence: "Santa Cruz Mayor Christopher Krohn made national headlines ... after he led the Santa Cruz City Council in presiding over a symbolic handout of marijuana to patients".

claims.claim: In 1988 a St. Louis University team including Allyn Howlett and her student William Devane characterized a cannabinoid receptor in the brain.
claims.evidence: Abstract via E-utilities: Devane WA ... Howlett AC, Mol Pharmacol 1988, "Department of Pharmacology, St. Louis University Medical School". ICRS memorial (https://www.icrs.com/in-memoriam-william-devane): Devane attended graduate school at Saint Louis University and "chose to work in Dr. Allyn Howlett's laboratory".

claims.claim: The 1988 paper was "the first characterization of a cannabinoid receptor in the brain".
claims.fix: No opened source states "first" (the abstract, the ICRS memorial and the Pertwee 2006 abstract were read; Europe PMC full text was unavailable). Reworded to "the seminal paper characterizing a cannabinoid receptor in the brain", ICRS's own word.
claims.evidence: "eventually published the seminal paper (Devane et al., 1988) - and in doing so initiated work by myriad laboratories world-wide to characterize localization and function of cannabinoid receptors".

claims.claim: Howlett later continued her work at Wake Forest.
claims.evidence: PubMed record via E-utilities (2024): "Howlett Allyn C, Department of Physiology and Pharmacology, Wake Forest School of Medicine, Winston-Salem, North Carolina".

claims.claim: Ziva Cooper directs the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids and studies how cannabis affects men and women differently.
claims.evidence: "Dr. Ziva Cooper is the Director of the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids"; funded projects on "differences between men and women in their response".

claims.claim: Cooper and Haney (Columbia, 2014): women matched with men for cannabis use gave higher ratings to some misuse-linked effects such as wanting to take the drug again; ratings of feeling high did not differ.
claims.evidence: Abstract via E-utilities: "Women reported higher ratings of abuse-related effects ['Take Again' and 'Good' (p<=0.05)] relative to men under active cannabis conditions but did not differ in ratings of intoxication"; Columbia University affiliations.

claims.claim: Sue Sisley, a physician and psychiatrist in Scottsdale, called federal research cannabis a "powdery mishmash of stems, sticks and leaves".
claims.evidence: "Sisley, a primary care physician and psychiatrist in Scottsdale, Arizona"; "The marijuana was a 'powdery mishmash of stems, sticks and leaves,' Sisley said."

claims.claim: She sued the DEA over its slow handling of research-grower applications; a 2020 suit settled when the government released the legal memo behind the delay.
claims.evidence: "they sued the DEA for not processing Sisley's application"; "That opinion was kept secret until Sisley and her legal team filed a lawsuit in March against the department, which settled this week with the release of the document." (April 2020)

claims.claim: Staci Gruber, Harvard Medical School psychiatry faculty, founded the MIND program at McLean Hospital, which uses observational studies, surveys and clinical trials.
claims.evidence: "associate professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School"; "founded the Marijuana Investigations for Neuroscientific Discovery (MIND) program ... through observational, longitudinal, and survey studies, as well as innovative clinical trials". Harvard Gazette 2017: "director of the MIND program ... at McLean Hospital".

claims.claim: California's Proposition 215 passed in 1996; Michigan voters approved a medical program in 2008 and adult use in 2018.
claims.evidence: MMMA approved Nov. 4, 2008; MRTMA effective Dec. 6, 2018; Prop 215 year per the American Prospect piece.

claims.claim: Wanda James, a military veteran, and her husband became the first African Americans to own a cannabis company in America in 2009, according to her CU regent biography; she later became the first Black woman elected to that board in more than 44 years.
claims.fix: none (the 'first' claim is attributed to the biography in the text)
claims.evidence: "Regent Wanda James became the first Black woman elected to the board in over 44 years."; "She served four years in the military."; "In 2009, James and her husband became the first African Americans to own a cannabis company in America."

claims.claim: A 2026 George Washington University study of 17 adult-use states with equity programs found women held from 22% of cannabis licenses (Illinois) to 44% (New Jersey) where reported.
claims.evidence: Abstract via E-utilities: "female-held licenses (Illinois: 22.0% to New Jersey: 44.0%)"; 17 states as of May 2025; GWU affiliations.

claims.claim: Industry surveys of women in executive roles have swung widely from year to year.
claims.evidence: MJBizDaily (Oct. 4, 2021): women held 22.1% of executive positions in 2021, versus "36.8% in 2019".

claims.claim: Gallup's combined 2023-2024 data: 15% of U.S. adults say they smoke marijuana, 17% of men and 11% of women; the question asks about smoking.
claims.evidence: "Fifteen percent of Americans report they smoke marijuana, according to combined Gallup data from 2023 and 2024."; "Men (17%) are more likely than women (11%) to say they smoke marijuana."

claims.claim: Every Michigan cannabis label carries a pregnancy and breastfeeding warning and names the producer and its state license number.
claims.evidence: "name and license number of the producer (and packager)"; "a boxed pregnancy and breastfeeding warning".

claims.claim: High Society: budtenders help customers look into brands; adults 21+ and medical card holders 18+ can shop with a valid ID; selection varies by store.
claims.evidence: "you need a valid government-issued ID proving you are 21 years or older"; "Individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases."; "Selection varies—check today's availability."

review.notes: Fact-check 2026-10-24 (low-risk article; no source cap): 32 claims checked, 3 fixed (unverifiable Physica hemp entry reworded; 'first' receptor characterization changed to ICRS's 'seminal'; 'city hall' location detail dropped). Sources list unchanged (14, all opened this session except the PubMed records, read through NCBI E-utilities). Extra evidence opened but not listed: ACLU release (WAMM's name), ICRS memorial (Devane in Howlett's lab), PubMed 37010379 (Howlett at Wake Forest), Crossref (Reynolds, Lancet 1890), MJBizDaily 2021 (executive share swing), Harvard Gazette 2017 (MIND at McLean).
